01: At 7:35 a.m., Army Signal Service observers across the country take the first synchronized weather readings and telegraph them to Washington: the start of the National Weather Service.
02: KDKA in Pittsburgh broadcasts the Harding-Cox presidential election returns, the night the pioneering station counts as its beginning.
Howard Hughes flies his giant wooden H-4 Hercules, the 'Spruce Goose', for about a mile at 70 feet over the water at Long Beach, California. It never flew again.
03: The Soviet Union launches Sputnik 2 with the dog Laika aboard, the first animal to orbit the Earth.
04: On election night the UNIVAC I computer, working from a small sample of the vote, predicts an Eisenhower landslide. CBS doubted it and aired a closer call. UNIVAC was right.
05: George Selden is granted U.S. patent 549,160 for a gasoline automobile, 16 years after he filed. Henry Ford beat the patent in court in 1911.
06: Edwin Armstrong presents his first paper on FM radio, a way to cut static with frequency modulation, to the Institute of Radio Engineers in New York.
07: At 9:22 a.m. Donald Smith drives the last spike of the Canadian Pacific Railway at Craigellachie, British Columbia.
08: Operation Torch: American and British forces land in French Morocco and Algeria, opening the U.S. fight against Germany and Italy.
09: The Great Lakes Storm of 1913, the 'White Hurricane', reaches its peak. In four days it destroyed 19 ships and killed more than 250 people.
10: The ore carrier Edmund Fitzgerald sinks in a storm on Lake Superior, about 17 miles from Whitefish Bay. All 29 men aboard are lost.
11: U.S. Route 66 is established, running from Chicago through St. Louis and on to the California coast.
The Armistice Day Blizzard strikes the Midwest after a mild morning. It kills 154 people, many of them duck hunters caught along the Mississippi River.
12: Space Shuttle Columbia launches on STS-2: the first time a crewed, reusable spacecraft returns to orbit.
13: The Holland Tunnel opens under the Hudson River between Jersey City and Manhattan: the world's first mechanically ventilated tunnel.
A Japanese submarine torpedoes the cruiser USS Juneau off Guadalcanal. Among the 687 men lost are the five Sullivan brothers of Waterloo, Iowa.
14: Eugene Ely flies a Curtiss biplane off a platform on the cruiser USS Birmingham: the first airplane takeoff from a ship.
Apollo 12 is struck by lightning twice in its first minute of flight. 'Try SCE to AUX' brings the data back, and the crew lands on the Moon five days later.
15: Edward Calahan unveils the first stock ticker in New York City, a telegraph printer that sends share prices over the wires.
Intel advertises the 4004 in Electronic News: 'a new era of integrated electronics'. It is the first microprocessor sold for general use.
16: John Ambrose Fleming applies for a U.S. patent on his 'oscillation valve', the two-electrode vacuum tube that became a foundation of radio.
17: The Suez Canal opens, joining the Mediterranean and the Red Sea. It cuts about 5,500 miles off the voyage between London and the Arabian Sea.
18: At noon, North American railroads switch to standard time zones, replacing some 50 separate railroad times.
19: Ford announces the end of the Edsel. Only 118,287 were built.
20: Microsoft releases Windows 1.0, a graphical environment that runs on top of MS-DOS.
21: Over Paris, Pilatre de Rozier and the Marquis d'Arlandes make the first untethered human flight: 25 minutes and about 5 miles in a Montgolfier hot-air balloon.
22: Pan American's flying boat China Clipper takes off from Alameda, California, for Manila with the first transpacific airmail.
23: After 76 hours of fighting, U.S. Marines declare Betio island in Tarawa Atoll secure. The 2nd Marine Division took more than 3,000 casualties.
24: Joseph Glidden of DeKalb, Illinois, receives his patent for barbed wire, the cheap fencing that changed ranching on the open range.
25: The U.S. Navy commissions USS Enterprise, the world's first nuclear-powered aircraft carrier.
26: J.B. Sutherland of Detroit is granted a U.S. patent for an 'Improved Refrigerator-Car', an early step toward shipping fresh food by rail.
27: New York's Pennsylvania Station opens in full, bringing Pennsylvania Railroad trains into Manhattan through tunnels under the Hudson River.
28: Frank Duryea wins the Chicago Times-Herald race, the first known automobile race in the U.S.: 54 miles through snow at an average of 5 miles per hour.
Hams span the Atlantic: Fred Schnell (1MO) and John Reinartz in Connecticut make the first two-way amateur contact with Leon Deloy (8AB) in France, on 110 meters.
29: Richard Byrd and three crewmen fly over the South Pole in the Ford Trimotor 'Floyd Bennett', an 18-hour, 41-minute round trip.
Atari releases Pong, the coin-operated table-tennis game that became the first commercially successful video game.
30: Samuel Clemens, later Mark Twain, is born in Florida, Missouri. He grew up in Hannibal and worked as a Mississippi riverboat pilot.
Britain's Flying Scotsman becomes the first steam locomotive officially recorded at 100 miles per hour.
